summary:
Piura is a department of Peru, and the sources contain no statute, enforcement record, court decision or incident specific to trans visitors in Piura. What binds Piura is the national framework of Peru in full. Nothing in the record marks Piura as either an aggravation of, or a refuge from, that framework, and no local mitigation, local protection ordinance or local enforcement practice is documented.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity. The national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The central mechanism is a restriction on restroom access. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex. Exceptions cover custody, cases where medical attention is required, and accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the draft also bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The measure stood at committee stage in February 2025. Its trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport.

LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho called the measure discriminatory and warned that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks. She stated that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

On 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions. A legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of the IDEHPUCP institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, published on 15 April 2025, holds that this violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors argue that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents mandated that restroom entry be determined by 'biological sex', barring trans people, including trans youth, from facilities matching their gender identity, and the same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Enforcement reaches private life: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Hate-crime protection was stripped from the Penal Code in 2017, when Congress voted to remove LGBT coverage from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. IDEHPUCP found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.
tangentialFactors:
The restroom restriction's practical reach depends on discretionary enforcement rather than on any inspection regime. Gianna Camacho's assessment is that access would turn on security staff's personal judgment, including identity-document checks, which means a trans visitor's experience at a mall, hotel, gym or transport hub in Piura varies with the individual on duty. No record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms supports the policy's stated rationale.

The policy's enforcement has already extended beyond state facilities. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a private gym operating under the same rule, and a television presenter invoked the men's room as a public taunt against a sitting member of Congress. Both episodes indicate that the restriction is treated as a general social norm, not a narrow administrative rule.

Peru's position is unusual in its subregion. Following the 2017 repeal, it is one of only three countries in South America, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, whose hate-crime law carries no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

The regional human-rights framework points the other way. Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights holds that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights, and the same Court's first torture-by-discrimination judgment, in the Azul Rojas Marín case, was reached through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. Both sit in tension with the domestic restroom statute.
localsOnly:
Residents of Piura live under the same national statute as visitors, and the sources record no local ordinance, prefecture directive or municipal practice that softens or sharpens it for people living there.

Healthcare access for trans residents improved on paper in June 2024, when Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. Whether Piura's regional health facilities have updated their forms and clinical language in line with that guidance is not sourced.

Recourse for residents is narrower than the statute suggests. Hate-crime provisions in the Penal Code have carried no LGBT anti-discrimination coverage since the 2017 repeal, and a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym enforcing the restroom policy.

Legal challenge remains available. A Lima constitutional court ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional in July 2025 after an activist legal challenge, and IDEHPUCP continues to publish constitutional analysis of the restroom provision, arguing that it breaches article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights.

Residents also face the speech provisions of the April 2025 law. Article 4 bans media and advertising content in vague terms, the minimum sentence for obscenity rose from three to four years, and Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Piura-specific enforcement data is sourced. Whether police, municipal inspectors or private security in Piura have applied the 'biological sex' restroom rule, and how often, is unresolved in the record.

The relationship between the February 2025 committee-stage bills 6506 and 8457 and the article 5 provision approved by the Plenary on 2 April 2025 is not fully traced in the sources; the inventory does not state whether the merged bills became the April law or proceeded separately.

The final status of the April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents after the July 2025 Lima constitutional ruling is not sourced. The ruling is described as annulling an anti-equality decree, and the sources do not establish whether it touches the restroom article.

Whether the dismissed gym complaint was appealed, and whether any further complaint has been filed in Piura, is not sourced. Nor is there any record of a trans visitor being refused restroom access, ID-checked or removed from a facility in Piura.

Figures on killings of transgender and gender-diverse people are national for 2020 to 2023 and are described by a report co-author as a sub-registry only; no regional breakdown for Piura is available, and the true scale of violence there is unresolved.
